title: Localization of the separable algebraic diagonal
statement: Let $k\subseteq k_1$ be a separable algebraic extension of fields [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. There exists a multiplicative subset $S\subseteq k_1\otimes_k k_1$ such that the multiplication homomorphism $\mu:k_1\otimes_k k_1\to k_1$, $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$, identifies $k_1$ with the localization $S^{-1}(k_1\otimes_k k_1)$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]; equivalently, $\mu$ is a localization map at $S$ (every element of $S$ maps to a unit of $k_1$; every element of $k_1$ equals $\mu(x)\mu(s)^{-1}$ for some $x\in k_1\otimes_kk_1$ and $s\in S$; and every $x\in k_1\otimes_kk_1$ with $\mu(x)=0$ satisfies $sx=0$ for some $s\in S$).

source.place: Tag 0C2X, lemma-separable-algebraic-diagonal, statement and proof (finite separable case via a primitive element and the general algebraic-union argument)

proof.text: Put $R=k_1\otimes_k k_1$, the commutative ring with $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$ and unit $1\otimes1$ of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] (1); by (2) of the same node, applied to $f=g=\mathrm{id}_{k_1}$, the multiplication $\mu$ is a homomorphism of $k$-algebras. Put $S=\{s\in R:\mu(s)\ne0\}$. Since $\mu(1)=1$ and $k_1$ is a field, $1\in S$ and $s,t\in S$ imply $\mu(st)=\mu(s)\mu(t)\ne0$. Thus $S$ is multiplicative in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization], and each $\mu(s)$ is a unit. Also $\mu$ is surjective, since $\mu(c\otimes1)=c$ for $c\in k_1$. It remains to show that every element of $\ker\mu$ is killed by an element of $S$.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, lemma-separable-algebraic-diagonal, general-case paragraph: choose denominators whose multiplication images are invertible

proof.text: Fix $x\in R$ with $\mu(x)=0$. By the generation clause of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] write $x=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\otimes b_i$, absorbing any $k$-scalar coefficients into the $a_i$. Let $E=k(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\subseteq k_1$. Each $b_i$ is algebraic over $k$ by [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], so [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-generators-finite-extension] makes $E/k$ finite. Every element of $E$, being an element of $k_1$, is algebraic with separable minimal polynomial over $k$ by the same definition; thus $E/k$ is separable algebraic. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-separable-primitive-element] to obtain $\alpha\in E$ with $E=k(\alpha)$. This also covers an empty tensor sum: then $E=k$ and a primitive element may be $0$.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, proof: finite separable case uses Fields Tag 030N (lemma-primitive-element); general case uses the union of finite subextensions, with finiteness supplied by Fields Tag 09GH (lemma-algebraic-finitely-generated)

proof.text: Let $P\in k[T]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. By [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], $P(\alpha)=0$ and $P$ is separable. The last clause of [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-polynomial-quotient-field-iso] says that $k(\alpha)=\{g(\alpha):g\in k[T]\}$; hence choose $g_i\in k[T]$ with $b_i=g_i(\alpha)$. View $P,g_i$ also in $k_1[T]$ by the coefficient inclusion and set $F(T)=\sum_i a_i g_i(T)$. Put $t=1\otimes\alpha\in R$, and evaluate polynomials in $k_1[T]$ in the commutative ring $R$ (the map $c\mapsto c\otimes1$ is the ring homomorphism $\iota_{k_1}$ of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] (1)) by sending a coefficient $c$ to $c\otimes1$ and $T$ to $t$. The coefficientwise formulas of [def-weil-polynomial-ring] and tensor bilinearity [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] give $F(t)=x$ and $F(\alpha)=\sum_i a_i b_i=0$: for $g_i=\sum_j c_{ij}T^j$ with $c_{ij}\in k$, one has $(c_{ij}\otimes1)t^j=1\otimes(c_{ij}\alpha^j)$ and therefore $(a_i\otimes1)g_i(t)=a_i\otimes b_i$.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, finite separable paragraph: the polynomial presentation of the tensor square; Fields Tags 09G1 (lemma-field-extension-generated-by-one-element) and 09GN (lemma-degree-minimal-polynomial) give polynomial representatives

proof.text: We spell out the polynomial factorization used in the source. For $G(T)=\sum_j c_jT^j\in k_1[T]$ define $D_G(T)=\sum_{j\ge1}c_j\sum_{h=0}^{j-1}T^{j-1-h}\alpha^h$. The finite geometric-sum identity $(T-\alpha)\sum_{h=0}^{j-1}T^{j-1-h}\alpha^h=T^j-\alpha^j$ gives $G(T)-G(\alpha)=(T-\alpha)D_G(T)$ by summing coefficients, using [def-weil-polynomial-ring]. Since $P(\alpha)=F(\alpha)=0$, take $Q=D_P$ and $H=D_F$ to get $P=(T-\alpha)Q$ and $F=(T-\alpha)H$. Evaluating the explicit sum for $Q$ at $\alpha$ gives $Q(\alpha)=\sum_{j\ge1}j p_j\alpha^{j-1}=P'(\alpha)$, where $P=\sum_j p_jT^j$ and the derivative is the coefficient formula of [def-pc-separable-polynomial]. No division algorithm or assertion about tensor-product injectivity is needed for these identities.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, finite separable paragraph: factor P=(x-alpha)Q; the finite geometric-sum calculation supplies the omitted factorization details

proof.text: By the separability of $P$, [def-pc-separable-polynomial] gives $U,V\in k[T]$ with $UP+VP'=1$. Evaluate this identity at $\alpha\in k_1$. Since $P(\alpha)=0$, it reads $V(\alpha)P'(\alpha)=1$. Thus $P'(\alpha)\ne0$, and Step 4 gives $Q(\alpha)\ne0$. This argument works in positive characteristic as well: the integer factors in the derivative are interpreted in the field, and the Bezout identity is what guarantees nonvanishing.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, finite separable paragraph: separability implies Q(alpha) is nonzero

proof.text: Set $s=Q(t)\in R$, with evaluation as in Step 3. Since $\mu(c\otimes1)=c$ and $\mu(t)=\alpha$, one has $\mu(s)=Q(\alpha)\ne0$, so $s\in S$. In $R$, $P(t)=\sum_j(p_j\otimes1)(1\otimes\alpha^j)=1\otimes\sum_jp_j\alpha^j=1\otimes P(\alpha)=0$, using the balancing relations of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] since $p_j\in k$. Evaluating the identities from Step 4 in the commutative ring $R$ of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] (1), where $\mu$ is a ring homomorphism by (2) now gives $sx=Q(t)F(t)=Q(t)(t-\alpha\otimes1)H(t)=P(t)H(t)=0$. Thus every $x\in\ker\mu$ has the required annihilator in $S$. Only the finitely many right tensor factors of $x$ entered the finite subextension; no finiteness assumption on $k_1/k$ has been used.

source.place: Tag 0C2X, finite separable localization calculation and general-case paragraph: every kernel element is killed by a denominator from a finite stage

proof.text: Using the fraction construction of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] with $M=R$, define $\phi:S^{-1}R\to k_1$ by $r/s\mapsto\mu(r)\mu(s)^{-1}$. If $r/s=r'/s'$, there is $u\in S$ with $u(s'r-sr')=0$; applying $\mu$ and cancelling the nonzero factors proves equality of the proposed values. The fraction addition and multiplication formulas show that $\phi$ is a ring homomorphism, and $\phi(r/1)=\mu(r)$. It is surjective because $c=\phi((c\otimes1)/1)$. If $\phi(r/s)=0$, then $\mu(r)=0$, so Step 6 supplies $u\in S$ with $ur=0$. The fraction equality criterion gives $r/s=0$. Thus $\phi$ is injective as well, hence an isomorphism identifying $\mu$ with $R\to S^{-1}R$. In particular the three explicit localization conditions in the statement all hold (the fraction representation of $c$ uses numerator $c\otimes1$ and denominator $1$).

source.place: Tag 0C2X, final paragraph: deduce the localization identification from surjectivity and annihilation of the kernel, written directly on fractions

lean.statement: theorem separableAlgebraicDiagonalLocalization (k : Type u) (k₁ : Type v) [Field k] [Field k₁] [Algebra k k₁] [Algebra.IsSeparable k k₁] : ∃ S : Submonoid (k₁ ⊗[k] k₁), (∀ s : k₁ ⊗[k] k₁, s ∈ S → IsUnit (Algebra.TensorProduct.lmul' k s)) ∧ (∀ c : k₁, ∃ x : k₁ ⊗[k] k₁, ∃ s : k₁ ⊗[k] k₁, s ∈ S ∧ c = Algebra.TensorProduct.lmul' k x * (Algebra.TensorProduct.lmul' k s)⁻¹) ∧ (∀ x : k₁ ⊗[k] k₁, Algebra.TensorProduct.lmul' k x = 0 → ∃ s : k₁ ⊗[k] k₁, s ∈ S ∧ s * x = 0)
